catalog_quote: In Asturian, the stress does not always appear on the same syllable in words with the same structure. There are three stress patterns: words with the lexical stress on the last syllable (oxytone), the penultimate syllable (paroxytone) and the antepenultimate syllable (proparoxytone). Though scarce, there also are words with enclitic parts that can have the stress on the syllable before the antepenultimate one, e.g. déxanoslo [ˈdeʃanozlo] ‘lend it to us’. The syllable nucleus is always a vowel. The stress opposition has a contrastive function and is very productive since it differentiates the meaning between lexical sets, e.g. llima [ˈʎima] ‘lime’ llimá [ʎiˈma] ‘slug’, and also between morphological forms, e.g. atopo [aˈtopo] ‘I find’ atopó [atoˈpo] ‘s/he found’. Phonetically, the stress is manifested in a pitch prominence. This is generally accompanied by a greater duration, and sometim…

new_statements.quote: N'asturianu l'acentu ye llibre (xinte / xinté), anque en xeneral asóciase nuna mesma pallabra siempre a una sílaba fixa; ye perestraño que la sílaba tónica se tresllade dientro la pallabra. De toes maneres, sí ye normal que los sufixos o les desinencies verbales faigan que l'acentu camude de sílaba. Exemplos: furacu, pero furaquín; lleche, pero llecheru; Payares, pero payariegu; yo falo, pero nós falamos; mancar, pero mancadura [p. 65] ... Según el llugar onde tea asitiada la sílaba tónica, les pallabres tóniques clasifíquense n'agudes, llanes y esdrúxules. [...] Esisten tamién pallabres peresdrúxules, que son aquelles nes que la tonicidá s'asitia na sílaba anterior a l'antepenúltima. Exemplos: enredábenteles, cantábenvosla, enfocicábase-yos. [p. 66]
new_statements.translation: In Asturian the accent is free (xinte / xinté), although in general within a given word it is always associated with a fixed syllable; it is very rare for the stressed syllable to shift within the word. All the same, it is normal for suffixes or verbal endings to make the accent change syllable. Examples: furacu but furaquín; lleche but llecheru; Payares but payariegu; yo falo but nós falamos; mancar but mancadura [p. 65] ... According to where the stressed syllable sits, stressed words are classified as oxytone (agudes), paroxytone (llanes) and proparoxytone (esdrúxules). [...] There are also pre-proparoxytone words (peresdrúxules), in which stress sits on the syllable before the antepenult. Examples: enredábenteles, cantábenvosla, enfocicábase-yos. [p. 66]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Asturian has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; this normative grammar supplies the rule: free/contrastive stress within the last three syllables, plus verb+enclitic pre-antepenult stress. Describes the Academia's standard Asturian.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is free (lexically determined and contrastive: xinte vs xinté), fixed for each lexeme, and may fall on the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable; stress before the antepenult occurs only in verb forms with enclitic pronouns. Stress is realised as greater intensity (loudness) on the syllable nucleus; in a diphthong or triphthong it falls on the open vowel. Derivational suffixes and verbal endings shift the stress position.
new_statements.exceptions: Unstressed (átones) word classes: articles, relatives, object clitic pronouns, prepositions and conjunctions lean on the stress of an adjacent word (sec. 2.1.2, p. 66). Monosyllables are described only for orthography (sec. 3.6.1, p. 69). Sequences of two close vowels (diptongos indiferentes: viuda, suizu, Lluis) may take stress on either vowel (p. 65).
new_statements.identity_note: ALLA 2001 describes the codified standard Asturian (normative grammar of the Academia de la Llingua Asturiana), which the catalog's 'Asturian' = astu1245 covers; it does not single out a dialect. García Arias 2003 is a historical grammar of Asturian (unopened).
